trails.title: An Unfinished Book
trails.description: Writing a book is sometimes akin to having a conversation with yourself.

content.text:
After that, the "Storm" brought the world to the 1990s.
Ms. Isolde readily accepted treatment. Ms. Kakania has been traveling the world, striving to change it. She quickly adapted to the new era and read many books. I also gave her plenty of recommendations.
It is worth noting that after the Vienna incident, Ms. Semmelweis became a vampire. This came as a massive surprise to everyone, but it also fascinated me—like reaching the payoff for a story's foreshadowing. After making many sincere requests, I got permission to read the beginning of her story. It is a complex tale, one that leaves you pondering incessantly about how it ends. However, if I were to retell the whole story here, this book would end up three times thicker. I would like to thank my mentor, Madam Hofmann, for showing me how to keep things concise in situations like this.
...
The world has traveled to 1920, but the war has not ended. It all feels like a continuation of that chaotic day. I heard Ms. Kakania was dejected the whole day, but she quickly returned to her mission from the Field Agent Administration. Even after crossing two eras, her tenacious spirit has not dampened at all. It seems that spirit has affected me, too: I find myself constantly thinking about what I can do. Thus, I have decided to write this book to organize my thoughts, in the hopes that I will find a conclusion before the final draft.
...

trails.title: Researcher Onboarding Guide
trails.description: The more eccentrics there are, the more guides there are.

content.text: Beginner's Guide to Ciphers: Vigenère Edition

To prevent Laplace employees from falling victim to pranks from colleagues and to avoid research delays from being unable to break codes, we are distributing this Beginner's Guide to Ciphers: Vigenère Edition.
The Vigenère cipher can be seen as an upgrade to the Caesar cipher, turning the simple shift of a single alphabet into shifts across multiple alphabets to increase complexity. For more on the Caesar cipher, see the Caesar Cipher Edition.
The main difference between the Vigenère and Caesar ciphers is that in the Vigenère cipher, the relationship between the ciphertext and plaintext letters isn't one-to-one, making the key harder to figure out. However, since it still follows patterns, you can still find repeating ciphertext segments. By using high-frequency words in common language, you can guess the plaintext for specific segments of ciphertext, deduce the key length from the spacing between repeats, and analyze the key.
However, if you don't have much text, this can be difficult. In these situations, you should use other methods to guess the key. The personality, past, and writing habits of the person who made the code are important clues. Here is a list of people at Laplace who are very likely to play pranks with ciphers:

Adler, Ulrich, X, Richard, Dawkins, Victor ...

If you encounter a prank, consider these suspects first. If you can't crack the code, confront the suspects directly and ask them to stop the prank. If a suspect denies involvement, try to force them to decode it for you. It doesn't matter whether they're really the culprit or not.

items.text: Hofmann Family Home
I'm heading out.
You can heat up the leftovers in the fridge for lunch. Did you hear that, Adler?

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: What's the appeal of the mountaineering club, anyway?

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: At this point, even the neighbors are saying, "Looking for Greta? She's probably gone mountain climbing."

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: Or rowing.
The young woman at the door has already laced up her shoes. She stamps her feet on the mat.
She shoulders her hiking pack and glances back at her brother as she rises.

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: Would you like to come?

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: Last time you joined me on the Karwendel climb, before we'd even made it back, you said you'd never participate in any weekend sports events ever again.

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: Chess, swimming, or doing those math problems you love—they're all worthy pastimes. There's no need to follow me.

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: I only came here to get a glass of water!

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: Haha, sure. By the way, I need your help with something.
Greta tosses him a set of keys.
He catches them, his eyes never leaving the crossword in his newspaper.

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: What are you poring over now? Planning to lock up Papa's cigarette cabinet behind a code again?

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: That was just a Vigenère cipher. A beginner's puzzle.

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: Mhm. Anyway, if you have the time, could you mow the lawn in the back garden? It would make Mama and Papa happy.

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: And you know, I've never asked—what's got you so dead-set on "Laplace"?

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: There are plenty of outstanding research facilities to choose from. Why them?

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: Because I believe we share the same ideals.

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: Hmm?

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: The seriousness in his tone makes her pause. Her hand lingers over the doorknob.

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: There must be a theory that unifies everything in the universe.

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: Because every puzzle has a solution.

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: The world is like a crossword. If you follow the clues, you'll arrive at an answer. The only answer. An established theory.

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: It's simple. Clear. Rational.

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: Codes simply rearrange symbols according to a set of rules. Identify these rules, and you can decipher it. If we don't have an answer, it doesn't mean it doesn't exist, but rather that we haven't discovered it yet.

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: I've attended lectures at Laplace. Their researchers firmly believe they can discover the truth. It's utter conceit.

items.speaker: Adler
items.text: But that's the way it should be.
Greta nods and opens the door with a smile.

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: I see. Don't worry. I'm sure you'll receive an invitation from them soon enough.

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: I've asked around. They all said age is no matter, nor whether or not you're an arcanist.

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: Laplace opens its doors to geniuses. That's the only requirement.

items.speaker: Greta
items.text: Won't be any trouble for you, dear brother.
He crouches and sets the flowers down before the headstone.
They join other bouquets. White chrysanthemums now spill over the edge of the stone and onto the grass.
Hallway, Foundation
Their tense, fruitless meeting finally ends. Enigma stands in the busy hall, adrift.
Staff members rush past without noticing him, arms full of files, each load heavier than the last.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Ha, talk about using a sledgehammer to crack a nut.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: What a meaningless waste of resources.
*beep—beep—*
The communicator rings just in time, cutting off his lingering contempt for the meeting he'd suffered through just half an hour ago.

items.speaker: Pointer
items.text: Adler. If you aren't dealing with anything urgent, please return to Laplace as soon as possible.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: What happened?

items.speaker: Pointer
items.text: We've made some new discoveries regarding the tower's core.

items.speaker: Pointer
items.text: It changes when observed. We need to come up with a new plan.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Many people remember you.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Even Musae III's toybox has a chunk of data still diligently simulating your stubbornness. Heh.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: But I'm sure you don't want to hear me prattle on about the past.
Whether to convince himself or to push something away, Enigma searches his cluttered thoughts for something else to say.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: The tower in the toybox, the Tower of Babel we used to solve the "language disorder"—it isn't the final solution.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Yes, people are able to use verbal communication to understand each other again. Unprecedented, I know.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: But this has come at a cost. The pieces' cognitive processes have all unified under the same model.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Unanimous agreement, unanimous objection—can this even be considered communication?
He's been staring at the engraved letters for so long that they've started to look strange. It's like this is all some sort of dream.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Ulrich and I each set off on our own expeditions. But in the end, we both decided to destroy the tower and take its core.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: So, now we have a new problem to solve—the core has a combination lock.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: And I can't make heads or tails of it.
The headstone offers only silence. Though, that doesn't stop Enigma from working out what Greta's response may have been.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Ha, I know. You wouldn't understand.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: This is supposed to be my specialty. Finding clues, cracking codes—all it takes for me is time.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: But my mind's gone rusty. Even my own thoughts have become unreliable.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: I haven't done any research of my own in a long time. Oh, no, just pointless meetings and endless paperwork.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Trivial, inconsequential matters have absorbed my every waking moment, grinding the old gears in my head to a halt. I can almost hear them creaking when I try to get them turning again.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Perhaps, I've lost the talent I once had.
He nods with a bitter smile.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Hah, maybe one day soon, I'll be using one of X's inventions. Even his simplest robots couldn't do any worse than me.
The white chrysanthemums whisper in the drifting wind, and as he falls silent, the world's sounds close in around him.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: Oh! Mr. Enigma.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: You're here too.
He turns toward the voice. Greta's mentee stands behind him, arms full of documents and flowers.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: I have a meeting with the Foundation. This was on the way.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: You're here to see her again.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: Yes, I've brought some new manuscripts for her to see.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: These manuscripts ... I'm going to submit them to the Daydream Post, but I'm not sure whether I'll be rejected again.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: I used a different recording technique this time, based on the feedback Madam Hofmann gave me once.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: So I wanted to show them to her before I got an answer from the magazine.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: I hope she can see that I've finally figured out what to do with my limitless "reading."

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: Instead of focusing on how much I can "read," I've decided to focus on the specific truths I can glean from them to record the story of the "Storm."
Enigma steps aside. Marcus lays the flowers on top of the documents and sets them both before the headstone.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: Without betraying my own principles or Madam Hofmann's teachings, I've managed to find a recording technique that can realize my dream.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: Of course, it's definitely lacking in a lot of ways.
Marcus manages to say what she means, though not without stumbling over herself.
She doesn't know Enigma well. Greta was the lone thread that connected them.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: Actually, Mr. Enigma, I never thought you'd come here. Oh, I-I don't mean that as a criticism! I only mean, I understand how you were feeling.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: But I suppose, now you're here, you've found an answer to that question?
Marcus chooses her words with care.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Not yet.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: But staying like this isn't going to help me think, either.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: Mm. Well, "reading" takes time. And so does seeking proof.

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Perhaps. You probably have a lot to say to her. I'll get out of your way.
Enigma reaches into his pocket and feels the cold metal tube in his palm.
He rummages in the other.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: What's wrong, Mr. Enigma?

items.speaker: Enigma
items.text: Nothing. Here.
Marcus opens her hands. Enigma drops something into them and turns to leave.
She looks down. She knows these candies well. Similar ones could always be found in her mentor's pockets.
The sharp, cold scent makes her blink.

items.speaker: Marcus
items.text: Oh, mints.
